This lack of proof-reading ability also allows retroviruses like HIV to replicate within a host cell. Explanation: Denaturation is the process of disrupting the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases in a double-stranded molecule of DNA. When heated, the two strands separate and form individual single-stranded DNA molecules. This allows the DNA to be more accessible to other enzymes and proteins that may interact with it. One example of this is the use of PCR (polymerase chain reaction) which relies on the ability to separate the two strands of DNA. This process is also used in gel electrophoresis where the DNA is loaded into wells and separated based on its size. In order to visualize the DNA, ethidium bromide or SYBR Green are added. These intercalating agents bind non-covalently between the base pairs of the single-stranded DNA forming a complex. This makes the DNA easier to see under UV light as it fluoresces. Another example would be using agarose gels for separating DNA fragments by size. The DNA is loaded into these wells and then run through an electric field. The gel will allow the movement of small molecules like water but not larger ones like DNA. When the DNA moves through the gel, it leaves behind a trail of fluorescent dye called ethidium bromide. This allows us to visualize the different bands of DNA that have been separated. Finally, one last example would be using restriction enzymes to cut specific sequences out of the genome. Restriction enzymes recognize particular sites in the DNA sequence and cleave them at those locations. Once they have done their job, we can remove them from our sample so that only the desired section remains intact. All three examples above rely heavily on the fact that when denatured, DNA becomes more accessible than when it's double-stranded. By breaking up the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, we open up new possibilities for studying and manipulating our genomes.
